input.question: Low earth orbit speed is 15,430 mph to 17,450 mph. Escape speed must be higher. Why did it take Apollo missions three days to reach the moon, then, when it is only ~238,900 miles away?
input.ground_truth: Remember [Kepler's 2nd Law](_URL_1_) - orbits sweep out equal areas in equal time. For an elliptical orbit, such as a transfer orbit to the Moon, the effect of this law is that as you get further from Earth, the distance traveled along your orbit in a given time is less. So as the Apollo missions were traveling out to the Moon, they were constantly slowing down the entire time. By the time they were close enough to the Moon for the Moon's gravity to start pulling them inwards, [they were only traveling about 1113m/s](_URL_0_), or 2,489 mph.

Okay, let’s imagine you want to throw a ball really far, all the way to your friend who is standing on the other side of a big field.

If you just throw the ball gently, it will fall down before it gets there.  
If you throw it really, really hard (faster than just “orbit” speed), it can escape the field and never come back—that’s like “escape speed.”

But if you want your ball to go to your friend and *stop* there, you can’t just throw it super hard. You have to throw it just right so it goes in a big curve (that’s like going into orbit), but not so fast that it flies away forever.

Now, the Moon is really far away—about 239,000 miles! Even though the Earth is spinning fast and the rocket goes really fast (like 17,500 miles per hour!), it’s not going straight to the Moon. Instead, it goes in a big, looping path around the Earth first, kind of like swinging around on a rope.

Also, the rocket doesn’t just go straight to the Moon. It has to line up just right, and it doesn’t go in a straight line—it goes in a big curve called an “orbit.” Plus, it needs to slow down a little at the end to actually *land* on the Moon, not just zoom past it.

So, even though the Moon is “only” 239,000 miles away, the rocket can’t just go straight there at top speed. It takes time to get into the right path, and it has to travel along a big curve, not a straight line. That’s why it takes about three days for the Apollo missions to get to the Moon!
